title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Hanani
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Hanani

He wasn’t a king.
He wasn’t a warrior.
He walked in, told the truth, and got punished for it.

In 2 Chronicles 16:7–9, Hanani the seer confronts King Asa after Asa trusted political deals instead of the Lord. No flattery. No soft edit. Just a burning word from God: “For the eyes of the LORD range throughout the earth to strengthen those whose hearts are fully committed to him.”
That line will shake you if you let it.

Because Hanani reminds us that God is not impressed by our image, our connections, or our survival strategies. He is looking for a heart fully His. Asa had history with God. Victories. Testimonies. Altars. And still, when pressure came, he leaned on human help more than divine faithfulness.

Not open rebellion at first.
Just misplaced trust.

And here’s what we miss: Hanani stands in Scripture as the man who loved truth more than comfort. He spoke what was costly. Asa responded by imprisoning him. That’s how hard the flesh fights correction. Sometimes the messenger gets chained because the heart refuses to bow.
But the Gospel steps right into that tension.

Because all of us have a little Asa in us. We say we trust God, then panic and build our own rescue plans. We want God’s blessings without God’s rule. We resist the very voice sent to save us. And yet Jesus came for people exactly like that. He was the true faithful Witness, rejected by men, opposed for telling the truth, and nailed to a cross by hearts that would not repent. But through His death and resurrection, grace opened a door for the proud to become humble, the stubborn to become surrendered, and the guilty to become clean.

Hanani’s warning still echoes: Where is your trust really resting?
In influence?
In money?
In control?
In the backup plan you never surrendered to God?
Brother, sister—don’t overlook the characters who carry sharp truth. Sometimes the overlooked voice is the very mercy of God in disguise.

Repent while your heart is still soft.
Return while grace is still calling.
Jesus does not expose us to shame us. He exposes us to heal us.
The character I almost overlooked became a mirror I couldn’t escape.
